On December 1, 2020, Jackson signed with his hometown team, the [Detroit Pistons](/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons").[[35]](#cite_note-35) He made his debut for the team on December 23, logging 19 points and six rebounds in a 101–111 loss to the [Minnesota Timberwolves](/wiki/Minnesota_Timberwolves "Minnesota Timberwolves").[[36]](#cite_note-36) On April 1, 2021, Jackson scored a season-high 31 points, alongside four assists, in a 120–91 win over the [Washington Wizards](/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards").[[37]](#cite_note-37) He ended the 2020–21 season averaging a career-high 13.4 points per game.

On January 3, 2022, Jackson scored a season-high 24 points, alongside five rebounds, in a 115–106 win over the [Milwaukee Bucks](/wiki/Milwaukee_Bucks "Milwaukee Bucks").[[38]](#cite_note-38)

On February 10, 2022, Jackson and [Trey Lyles](/wiki/Trey_Lyles "Trey Lyles") were acquired by the [Sacramento Kings](/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings") in a four-team trade that sent [Marvin Bagley III](/wiki/Marvin_Bagley_III "Marvin Bagley III") to the Pistons.[[39]](#cite_note-39) The move reunited Jackson with former Suns teammates [Richaun Holmes](/wiki/Richaun_Holmes "Richaun Holmes") and [Alex Len](/wiki/Alex_Len "Alex Len").

On August 31, 2022, Jackson signed with the [Toronto Raptors](/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors").[[40]](#cite_note-40) He was waived on October 14.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

On January 24, 2023, Jackson signed with the [Stockton Kings](/wiki/Stockton_Kings "Stockton Kings").[[42]](#cite_note-42) He was waived four days later.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

With Everest to the north and [Nuptse](/wiki/Nuptse "Nuptse") to the west, Lhotse forms the apex of the massive horseshoe-shaped arc of the Everest [massif](/wiki/Massif "Massif"). The title of **president of King’s College** was created in 1754 by the original [royal charter](/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") for the university, issued by [George II](/wiki/George_II_of_Great_Britain "George II of Great Britain"), and the power to appoint the president was given to [an autonomous board of trustees](/wiki/Trustees_of_Columbia_University_in_the_City_of_New_York "Trustees of Columbia University in the City of New York"). The university suspended operations upon the outbreak of the [American Revolutionary War](/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), during which no individual served as president. When it was resuscitated by the [New York State Legislature](/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature "New York State Legislature"), the university was placed directly under the control of the [Board of Regents of the University of the State of New York](/wiki/Board_of_Regents_of_the_University_of_the_State_of_New_York "Board of Regents of the University of the State of New York"); its chancellor, [George Clinton](/wiki/George_Clinton_(vice_president) "George Clinton (vice president)"), served as the *de facto* president of Columbia University.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)
